original_value: Graph coloring is one of the most famous computational problems with applications in a wide range of areas such as planning and scheduling, resource allocation, and pattern matching. So far coloring problems are mostly studied on static graphs, which often stand in stark contrast to practice where data is inherently dynamic and subject to discrete changes over time. A temporal graph is a graph whose edges are assigned a set of integer time labels, indicating at which discrete time steps the edge is active. In this paper we present a natural temporal extension of the classical graph coloring problem. Given a temporal graph and a natural number ∆, we ask for a coloring sequence for each vertex such that (i) in every sliding time window of ∆ consecutive time steps, in which an edge is active, this edge is properly colored (i.e. its endpoints are assigned two different colors) at least once during that time window, and (ii) the total number of different colors is minimized. This sliding window temporal coloring problem abstractly captures many realistic graph coloring scenarios in which the underlying network changes over time, such as dynamically assigning communication channels to moving agents. We present a thorough investigation of the computational complexity of this temporal coloring problem. More specifically, we prove strong computational hardness results, complemented by efficient exact and approximation algorithms. Some of our algorithms are linear-time fixed-parameter tractable with respect to appropriate parameters, while others are asymptotically almost optimal under the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH).

result.paraphrase: Graph coloring is among the best-known computational problems, with applications spanning planning and scheduling, resource allocation, and pattern matching. Coloring problems have mostly been studied on static graphs so far, even though in practice data is often inherently dynamic and changes discretely over time. A temporal graph is one whose edges carry a set of integer time labels, specifying the discrete time steps at which each edge is active. In this paper, we introduce a natural temporal extension of the classic graph coloring problem. For a temporal graph and a natural number ∆, we seek a color sequence for every vertex such that (i) in every sliding window of ∆ consecutive time steps during which an edge is active, that edge is properly colored at least once within the window, meaning its endpoints receive different colors, and (ii) the number of distinct colors used overall is minimized. This sliding-window temporal coloring problem abstractly models many realistic graph coloring settings in which the underlying network evolves over time, such as assigning communication channels to moving agents dynamically. We give a detailed study of the computational complexity of this temporal coloring problem. In particular, we establish strong hardness results and also provide efficient exact and approximation algorithms. Some of these algorithms are linear-time fixed-parameter tractable for suitable parameters, while others are asymptotically almost optimal assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH).
